To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

HIT can be designed to facilitate the adoption of new knowledge into practice, and that the design and evaluation of such systems should be informed by a conceptual framework that incorporates the following key elements: 1) the need for a strong conceptual model that incorporates the cognitive, social and organizational dimensions of knowledge translation; 2) an understanding of the role of HIT in facilitating the adoption of new evidence into practice; 3) a clear understanding of the clinical context and its implications for the design of HIT tools;
HIT can be designed and implemented to catalyse changes in clinical practice, and that the design and implementation of such systems should follow an iterative, collaborative, user-centred process.

the design of HIT tools to support disease management must consider: the clinical context of the patient encounter, the cognitive context of the physician's decision-making, and the social context of the physician-patient relationship.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design of HIT to support clinical practice.
the design of HIT systems that will catalyse change and lead to improvements in the quality and safety of patient care.
the development of a HIT tool that will enable physicians and nurses to more effectively manage the health of patients.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HIT is not yet a panacea, but it is an essential component of any comprehensive approach to improving clinical outcomes and patient safety.
the evidence base for HIT to improve care is weak and needs to be strengthened, but there are promising signs of success.

HIT can be designed to improve the quality of care and patient outcomes, but this will require a new approach to the design of these systems, one that focuses on the needs of the end users and their workflow.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the design of health IT systems should be informed by a conceptual model that describes how information technology can be used to catalyse changes in physician behaviour, and that such systems should be designed to support the clinical workflow and be embedded into existing clinical systems.
we need to move beyond the current focus on HIT as a tool for information storage and retrieval and instead view it as a tool for knowledge translation.

we need to design HIT systems that are more closely aligned with the workflow and information needs of clinicians, and that can support the development of new care processes that are more effective than those in place today.
The main takeaway from our work is that
HIT tools need to be designed with the end user in mind, and that the end user should be involved throughout the entire design process.
HIT tools must be designed to fit the workflow of clinicians, not to fit the workflow dictated by the technology.
HIT systems must be designed to catalyse a change in clinical care and not merely to provide information.
